summary: The Longer Catechism, a standard Russian Orthodox statement of the faith, teaches that the Communion is a sacrament in which the believer, under the forms of bread and wine, partakes of the very Body and Blood of Christ to everlasting life. At the moment the words of institution are spoken in the Liturgy the bread and wine are changed, or transubstantiated, into the very Body and Blood of Christ; it adds, citing the Eastern patriarchs' exposition, that the word does not define how this happens, which only God understands. The catechism makes the Communion the chief part of divine service, asks believers to confess and communicate, and calls the faithful to receive at least once a year. The questions read do not address whether the Liturgy is a sacrifice.

points.question: What is the Communion?
points.answer: A sacrament in which the believer, under the forms of bread and wine, partakes of the very Body and Blood of Christ, to everlasting life. It forms the chief and most essential part of divine service.

points.question: What happens to the bread and wine?
points.answer: At the moment the words of institution are spoken, they are changed, or transubstantiated, into the very Body and Blood of Christ. Citing the Eastern patriarchs, the catechism says the word does not define the manner of the change, which only God understands; it means the bread truly, really and substantially becomes the very Body of the Lord.

points.question: Who may receive, and how often?
points.answer: Anyone who desires to approach is asked to prepare, and the Church calls those who live religiously to confess to a spiritual father and communicate several times a year, requiring all to receive at least once a year.
